Code Mode is an experimental new feature in Claude Code that can improve both speed and context efficiency when Claude needs to orchestrate multiple steps. Try it out and let us know what you think!

It enables Claude to perform multi-step tool calls by writing and running JavaScript. Rather than calling one tool at a time (e.g. Bash, Read, or Edit) and waiting to see the result before deciding what to do next, Code Mode allows Claude to write a simple script to run multiple commands in parallel, passing arguments and filtering outputs for subsequent tool calls to reduce context.

I'm excited about this work because Code Mode enables more efficient and streamlined multi-step coding flows. For example, rather than passing large amounts of raw search data into the context window or having to make a large number of sequential calls to perform the same refactoring across dozens of files, Claude can orchestrate these tasks programmatically in a single pass. 

Still, you will be able to interact with Claude as normal through natural prompts. And if you ever need to see the exact JavaScript that Claude generated, you can always use Ctrl+O to expand the collapsed Code rows in the transcript viewer.

One of the most exciting practical improvements from Code Mode is its ability to perform long-running operations, like running test suites or complex builds, as background processes. When Code Mode is running in either auto or bypassPermissions mode, scripts can run in the background for up to two hours. You can continue to interact with Claude and perform other work within the same session. The /tasks command provides complete transparency and control over background scripts.

Each tool call that is generated within a script is still governed by your current deny and ask permission policies, sandbox constraints, and PreToolUse hooks. Hooks can even be defined specifically for the REPL tool to inspect the generated JavaScript before running, or redact sensitive tokens from the output before reading it into the context. 

To enable Code Mode, just start your session with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 claude or set the environment variable in your ~/.claude/settings.json file.

Give it a try by running multi-file audits, batch edits, or any type of parallel search-and-filter operation. Code Mode is experimental and the team is actively iterating on it, so please run /feedback in your terminal to let us know what works well and where you hit any edges. 

Hope it's helpful!

IPO PRICE VS. OPENING PRICE: UNDERSTANDING HOW THE MARKET DETERMINES VALUE

One of the most important things to understand about an IPO is that the initial offering price and the actual opening market price are two different things.

The distinction comes down to how price discovery works.

Before public trading begins, the company and its underwriters determine the IPO price through a book-building process, taking into account investor demand, valuation expectations and the number of shares being offered.

However, that price does not dictate where the stock must trade once it enters the public market.

The opening price is established through an exchange auction, where buy and sell orders are collected and matched to determine an equilibrium price.

This process involves three important considerations:

1. Initial Offering Price

The underwriters establish the offering price based on institutional investor demand, the company's valuation and the supply of shares available.

2. Opening Auction and Price Discovery

The exchange evaluates incoming buy and sell orders, including their respective prices and quantities, to determine an opening price that clears the greatest executable volume.

3. First Executed Trade

Trading officially begins once the opening process is completed. For highly anticipated offerings, substantial order imbalances can extend this process beyond the regular market opening time.

Anthropic provides a practical example of this distinction.

Its shares were priced at $83 before public trading, but the first market price was $111.50, approximately 34% above the offering price.

That difference illustrates how market demand can produce a significantly different valuation once trading begins.

The key takeaway: An IPO price is the starting reference point, not a guaranteed market price. Understanding the auction mechanism helps traders interpret price movements rather than reacting blindly to the initial numbers.

You don't need long context!

NVIDIA researchers just published a paper questioning whether LLMs actually need huge context windows for long-running tasks.

The problem is that longer context is expensive.

As the context grows, every new token gets slower to generate, uses more memory, and costs more to serve.

In their measurements, going from a 16K to 256K context increased the cost per generated token by 3.6× for GLM 5.2, 5.6× for Kimi K2.6, and 7× for Qwen 3 Coder Next.

Their alternative is frequent context compaction.

Instead of carrying the entire conversation history through a long agent run, you keep a compact representation of the current task state and start a new context when needed.

For long documents, they use a similar idea: keep the documents outside the context and let the agent selectively read the parts it needs rather than loading everything at once.

They test this across software engineering, terminal tasks, tool use, retrieval, and long-document reasoning.

And the results are pretty interesting.

On long-horizon tasks, frequent compaction generally maintained or even improved task accuracy compared with keeping the full history.

They pushed this even further with Single-Action Compaction.

The model takes one action, observes the result, updates a compact semantic state, and then the entire conversation is discarded before the next action.

On Claude Opus 4.5, this preserved SWE-bench Verified performance and improved Terminal-Bench.

On GPT 5.6 Sol, the accuracy drop was only a few percentage points, while the median peak live context stayed around 7–9K tokens.

The paper takes this idea further and proposes Semantic State Space Models.

Instead of maintaining an ever-growing conversation history, the model carries a compact natural-language state between turns containing the information needed to continue the task.

This feels especially relevant for long-running agents.

You may not need to keep hundreds of thousands of tokens alive throughout the entire run. Keep the current state, retrieve what you need, compact aggressively, and continue.

Prompt, context, harness & loop engineering, clearly explained!

An agent is a while loop with four layers of engineering wrapped around it:

- Prompt engineering
- Context engineering
- Harness engineering
- Loop engineering

Each one wraps the last, and the model sits in the middle, so none of them compete with the others. Instead, they just zoom one level further out.

> Prompt engineering:

This defines the input the model sees on one call, often composed of a role, instructions, examples, and an output format.

The techniques here alter the internal computation and reasoning the model goes through due to the wording it sees:

- Chain-of-thought makes it work in steps before answering
- Few-shot examples define the format and the edge cases
- A JSON schema or XML tags make the output parseable by code
- Self-consistency samples a few chains and takes the majority

> Context engineering:

It's everything the model sees on a turn, not just the prompt. That includes the query, retrieved docs, memory, prior turns, and tool outputs from earlier steps.

The window is finite and fills up fast, so the engineering work is to rank inputs and cut everything that isn't pulling weight.

You do this by:

- Retrieving only the chunks relevant to the query, then reranking them
- Keeping key facts out of the middle, where accuracy drops
- Summarizing old turns, evict stale outputs, push big blobs to files

> Harness engineering:

It's the code around the model that defines the tools, parses the calls, retries on failure, and can route work to sub-agents so one handles retrieval and another handles code.

A verifier then grades the result by running tests, validating a schema, etc.

Prompt and context involve getting one call right. The harness involves everything that has to happen around that call for it to run in a real system.

> Loop engineering:

In the usual setup, you manage the outer loop, i.e, you write a prompt, read the turns the agent runs, write the next prompt, and repeat, while catching failures.

This layer hands that job to the agent itself. It kicks off on a schedule or an event, and runs many turns with no prompt in between.

A loop inherently doesn't know when it's finished. An agent can report that it's done and halt while the tests still fail. So the stop can't be the agent's word, but rather it has to be a real signal, like:

- A turn and token cap to stop stuck runs
- A no-progress detector to catch repeated calls
- A completion check to verify the goal with a separate model or a deterministic test

By this layer, you're operating on the whole run, so the engineering moves from writing each prompt to setting the goal and the stop conditions up front and letting it run.

A longer run also makes the cost of the layers underneath it grow.

When a tool returns a 50K-token response and nothing removes it, the model reads it again on every later call. Over a loop of twenty steps, one response turns into hundreds of thousands of tokens.

I wrote a full breakdown of where an agent's tokens actually go and how a harness keeps context flat, using TrueForge, an open-source harness that turns an LLM into a working agent.

GitHub repo: https://t.co/ZjePhhfKIh

(don't forget to star it ⭐ )

It covers offloading large tool outputs to files, subagents for context isolation, Code Mode for multi-tool joins, and compaction.

It also has a benchmark of three harnesses on the same 14 tasks, where TrueForge reached the same answers on about 40% of the tokens Claude Managed Agents used.

2124526033479045426.text:
By now many folks have seen the impressive visuals of Tesla’s v15 or the Tesla Reality View. One thing I noticed is how it can render roof tops and things that it cannot physically see.

So, I went down the rabbit hole with Grok. For those that want to geek out on this technology, read on my friend!

Basically, Reality View is not showing you a camera feed of the roofs. Instead, it is generating one.

The car’s cameras still only see what they can physically see mostly the sides of houses, the road, and whatever is in their field of view as you drive. What you see on the screen is a synthetic view created by the same neural network that is actually driving the car. Photons in, photons out!

It works by using the cameras feed into a shared vision system that builds an internal understanding of the 3D-world around the vehicle. It notes things like what’s occupied, what’s open, how things are moving. 

That understanding is then handed to a generative model that is trained to produce realistic images. The model is asked to render the scene as if a camera were floating above the car.

And here’s the wild part!

Because the model has learned what houses, roofs, trees, and streets generally look like from millions of real-world examples, it can complete the parts that the physical cameras never fully observed. It virtually completes the rendering. 

As the car moves, the system gets new partial views of the same buildings from different angles. The generative model keeps everything consistent.  It is constantly updating the roofs, walls, and shadows so they stay coherent instead of flickering or randomly changing. 

It’s the same idea behind AI imaging and video generators that are able to fill in missing parts of a photo or create a new camera angle that never existed. Except in this situation it is running in real time on the car and tied to what the driving system actually perceives.

Basically, the system is reconstructing a plausible, consistent 3D scene from the limited views it does have and then rendering that scene from an elevated virtual viewpoint. 

This is the first version of the Tesla Reality View and the rendering does have some glitches but expect this to only get better over time.

RAG vs. CAG, clearly explained!

RAG is great, but it has a major problem:

every query hits the vector DB. even for static information that hasn't changed in months.

this is expensive, slow, and unnecessary.

Cache-Augmented Generation (CAG) fixes this by letting the model keep static information in its key-value (KV) memory, which is what the model builds internally for every token it reads.

in fact, you can combine RAG and CAG for the best of both worlds.

here's how it works:

RAG + CAG splits your knowledge into two layers.

↳ static data (policies, documentation) gets cached once in the model's KV memory

↳ dynamic data (recent updates, live documents) gets fetched via retrieval

you get faster inference, lower costs, and less repeated work.

the trick is being selective about what you cache.

only cache static, high-value knowledge that rarely changes. cache everything and you'll hit context limits. separating "cold" (cacheable) and "hot" (retrievable) data keeps this system reliable.

you can start today. OpenAI and Anthropic already support prompt caching in their APIs.

one thing to know before you scale it.

prompt caching matches on an exact prefix, byte for byte. your cached layer only gets reused when it sits at the very front of the context in the same order every time.

↳ reorder two cached policy documents and both turn into a miss

↳ cache document A alone and document B alone, then query both, and the second one misses because the model computed its cached state without ever seeing the first

in production this looks like a small fraction of your cached blocks serving almost all the hits. the rest just sits there.

the way out comes from how attention behaves. tokens attend mostly to their own local neighborhood, and only a few reach across document boundaries. CacheBlend recomputes those few and reuses everything else from the separately cached documents.

multi-document queries run two to four times faster, quality holds, and order stops mattering.

it ships in LMCache, which is fully open source.

Frontier models can now propose technical social science research designs that experts grade more highly than the world's top political economist's---that's the finding from our new Free Systems eval, SnyderBench, in which we have PhD experts blind grade research proposals from AI models compared to papers written by Harvard political economist Jim Snyder (which the experts have not previously read). 

At the same time, we see no evidence that models can develop research ideas that experts rate as better overall contributions. They're getting better and better at the technical part of research, but not necessarily at the more subjective part.

This could be because human experts possess "judgment" that the models do not. 

It could also be that research "contribution" is so subjective that it doesn't actually point at any meaningful goal---consistent with this possibility, we find that our human experts don't agree with one another when rating project ideas for the strength of their contribution, with agreement rates barely higher than random chance. Perhaps social science research is what @alexolegimas might call a "relational good": something people value in part because it's produced by a human. We're not sure. 

This past January, I released the results of a pilot in which I had Claude Code replicate and extend a past empirical paper on vote-by-mail. 10 months later, it's stunning the amount of progress that's been made. It's no longer interesting to ask whether AI can collect data and run analyses automagically---we take that for granted---instead, the question is how much of the entire research loop AI can complete. Our tentative answer: AI can handle the technical aspects of empirical political economy research from end to end, devising the design and executing it, but for now, we still need humans to drive the agenda.

One boring but very consequential reason why models feel bad at non-verifiable tasks is they never put any effort into them.

Humans can take years writing a novel, or months thinking about a game spec - but ask a model and it will just spit something out. Ask it to formulate a new set of Millennium Prize Problems and it will slop something up in minutes. This feels closer to a mechanical failure that fundamental lack of capability. Seems like T3 Code reads your Claude and Codex credential files to hash your account IDs and send them with its telemetry.

Default-on usage stats are normal for dev tools, but reading another tool's auth files isn't.

And opting out isn't easy. There's no toggle and no config file. You have to set two environment variables in your OS:

export T3CODE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false
export T3CODE_OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true

Simpler fix, block the endpoint:
echo "0.0.0.0 https://t.co/B0yG7Lr4i2" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

The app still reads those auth files locally either way. I'll remove the telemetry entirely from my fork.

Here's the full list of what gets sent:

- Your OpenAI and Claude account IDs, hashed without salt, so anyone with your raw ID can match them back to you (see above).

- A permanent device ID, hashed, sent even if you never sign in.

- Your IP address with every batch, which gives a rough location.

- Custom model names, sent exactly as written. If one carries a private or internal name, that name gets out.

- A usage profile: which models you use, permission mode (such as full-access), token counts, run times and feature usage.
